speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: FELICITATIONS FROM LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON BEHALF OF HOUSE
speechtext: I understand that this is the Prime Minister's birthday. I should like to extend to my right hon. friend my best wishes for many happy returns of the day, and perhaps on this occasion he will allow me to speak for the house and to extend these wishes on behalf of us all.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: FELICITATIONS FROM LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON BEHALF OF HOUSE
speechtext: The very unusual and kindly act of the right hon. the leader of the opposition I shall not soon forget. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank him for having thought of so gracious an act as that which he has just now done and, more, for the felicitous terms in which he has expressed it. I have had a very interesting and very hardworking life; I have enjoyed the one and gained much experience from the other.
On the orders of the day:
On Saturday I directed a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in regard to Australian flour shipped from Southampton to Halifax. Has the minister any further information?

speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: There is no further information. There are a few small shipments coming in but nothing out of the usual. The necessary and, I think, effective steps have been taken to deal with the whole question and I may say that in this respect we are receiving the reasonable cooperation of the *Australian authorities.

My question was
directed to the minister in regard to this one shipment, which he said he would look into- a very large shipment from Southampton to Halifax.
I am sorry my hon. friend-
Don't be sorry for me.

Pardon me. I say I am sorry that my hon. friend persists in stirring up this question. I have stated repeatedly that with the very kind cooperation of the
Australian government the whole matter is being satisfactorily dealt with. The shipments are not large when one considers the movement of goods. The shipment he refers to is three hundred tons, not a large one. The matter is well in hand and is being most satisfactorily dealt with, and I do not think there is any need or occasion for agitation or alarm.
Does the minister suggest that I am agitating?
No, I said there was no need for agitation.
I hope the minister will not take any action that would tend to jeopardize the market for our own flour and wheat in Britain and other countries.
On the orders of the day:

I wish to ask a question of the Minister of the Interior. Yesterday I had the honour to be invited to the ordination of the first Indian priest in Caughnawaga, and while we were there the authorities were very anxious to know whether something could be done in the interests of hygiene. There is a very high death rate in that reservation. In the province of Quebec there are sanitary units and it would cost the Department of Indian Affairs only $150 a year, and the Quebec government could take charge of this reservation. I should be very much obliged if the minister, from his general estimates, could devote the necessary sum for hygiene purposes in this district.
Order.
With the kind permission of my hon. friends opposite I should like to present this matter to the minister.
If the hon. member is going to ask a question he should ask it. There is no motion before the house to justify a debate.
This is not a debate.
Will the hon. member proceed to ask his question?

I have no wish to embarrass the government, and the question is not asked for political purposes. It is only from a sentiment of humanity that I am putting the question.

I simply want to remind the minister that there is no sewer system there.
Hon. THOMAS G. MURPHY: (Minister of the Interior): I did not hear the question but I can only say that I shall be glad to give the hon. member's remarks consideration.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was going to ask the Prime Minister whether we would have an opportunity on the supplementary estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) of discussing the international wheat agreement. If we would at that time, then I would not raise the question now, but if we shall not have that opportunity on the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, then I propose to take the matter up now although I would prefer to do so on the estimates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: INTERNATIONAL WHEAT AGREEMENT-STATEMENT OF MR. MOTHERWELL

maintopic: INTERNATIONAL WHEAT AGREEMENT-STATEMENT OF MR. MOTHERWELL
speechtext:
As the house is aware, we have several times made the request from this side that we be given an opportunity of discussing the international wheat agreement, but the Prime Minister seemed to think we had already discussed it sufficiently in the interest of the question itself and of the country generally. Developments, however, have recently taken place in connection with the question, that render it necessary that we should have something to say about it before we prorogue. Because of that, rather than wanting to introduce the matter on going into supply, I thought maybe the Prime Minister would let it be discussed on the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but I believe my right hon. friend's decision is correct that the matter should be taken up now rather than on the estimates because there is no estimate dealing directly with the question and therefore permission to deal with it then might be denied.
The first step looking toward the failure of the international wheat agreement was in 1930 at the special session when the government of the day authorized imposing of an embargo on six or seven of the major exportable commodities of Russia. They did this in

none too delicate a way and it was accompanied by remarks that a great country like Russia could not be expected to entertain without some resentment. It seems to me that anyone who had any knowledge of international matters would know even at that time that embargoing the major exportable commodities of that great country was the last thing to do if we ever wanted to enter into an international trade agreement with Russia in regard to the production of wheat or any other commodity.
In 1931, the year following, there was an international conference at Rome respecting wheat. Russia had again come into the picture by that time as an exporter of wheat and the whole world was agog as to what was going to happen with Russia again exporting wheat, and at prices that some people said constituted dumping. The assemblage at Rome was brought about apparently with the hope that something might be done in the way of an international understanding about wheat. My recollection is that the Hon. Howard Ferguson, then and now High Commissioner for Canada, was Canada's representative at Rome and I think Doctor Riddell from Geneva was also there. The wheat pool had a representative there. Mr. Williams was there; I do not know whether he represented the pool or what, but Mr. Robertson was there on behalf of the wheat pool, as I understood. The conference was not very long under way when it became quite evident that very little was going to be done in the way of an international agreement. Russia was also represented. My recollection is-and I am subject to correction-that before the conference was very long under way, the wheat exporting countries were lined up on one side and the importing countries were lined up on the other. The conference adjourned with that line-up, the different countries not feeling very well disposed toward each other, the importing countries decided to reassemble in Paris under the leadership of the late Premier Briand and the others-the exporting countries

to reassemble in London under the leadership of the Canadian High Commissioner. This latter assembly was appointed more or less as a continuing committee to deal with this question, to dig into the matter of statistics and all that sort of thing, until finally in the following year, 1932, the Ottawa Imperial conference met in this capital city. The question of an international agreement with respect to wheat did not come up very prominently at that conference but the question of British preference in regard to wheat did. We do not need to go into that matter; the Prime Minister took the ground at that

Supply-International Wheat Agreement
time that the preference was intended not to raise the price of wheat but rather to give Canada a sheltered or secured market in Great Britain which objective subsequent events do not seem to prove, has yet been attained.
In the year following that, the big world international conference at London was convened where sixty or more countries were represented. Surely something was now going to be done with regard to not only an international wheat agreement but many other matters. It was thought the world was ready for a rest in connection with tariff increases and the very knotty problem of exchange was also to the fore, Great Britain having gone off the gold standard in the meantime in September, 1931. I do not need to tell the house what happened at that great international London conference which was very imposing. It was thought there were great possibilities in it, but President Roosevelt apparently got a new light as to what his duties were and something suddenly arose with regard to the conference proper, that is so far as the two features I have mentioned were concerned. Out of that international conference proper, that is the one consisting of some sixty countries, was developed what might be called an auxiliary conference. It was practically the same conference but there was a subconference-I use that term for want of a better-comprising some twenty-one countries that were interested in either buying or selling wheat. According to my recollection my good friend the Prime Minister was chairman of that conference. I have no notes before me; I am speaking from memory and it will not aggrieve me at all if I run off the track and somebody sets me right; but I remember the right hon. gentleman was chairman; I may say that he was the head, the tail and the middle of that conference. We have just been passing felicitations about my good friend's birthday and this would be a nice time to make the remark that no matter whether it was a world conference or a smaller local one, my right hon. friend was never in it for ten minutes or at least half an hour before he was the centre of attraction and was pretty much in control of the conference especially when he was chairman. Naturally that would be the case. I can imagine him being there when he would be in the limelight, the central and the most brilliant member of that conference; I do not know anyone who would be more so. Had it not been for his great energy, personality and perseverance there would not on that occasion have been any international wheat agreement. But when we know him as we do and the masterful manner in which he 74726-290 i
takes up a question, especially one with which he was thought by the other countries to be pretty well familiar, there was nothing else to it but to go ahead with his great driving force behind the project and the conference. It has often been said that this was the one redeeming feature of the international conference consisting of sixty countries, that convened there some weeks or months previously. Therefore, when my right hon. friend returned from that conference in London with the laurels of what seemed to be a considerable victory on his brow, he might be pardoned for making some pretty strong claims on its behalf and at least he might have been expected to ask the concurrence and approval of this house in his wonderful achievement. But that has not been don^ yet. And we know why it has not been none. Anyhow the Prime Minister came back and made a very extraordinary speech in Winnipeg before a body of young business men, saying in regard to the agreement: What is there to do in this world regarding the increasing and embarrassing wheat carry-over? but just what business men are doing? When they found their shelves were full of goods for which there were not enough buyers they reduced their inventories, that is reduced orders for goods from the manufacturers until the shelves were lightened. We have to remember that that illustration was given before a body of business men; it was the sort of illustration that would appeal to them. It took like hot cakes, as the saying is, with them, and it seemed a reasonable thing to suggest that the farmers do the same in their wheat production policies. That was the way he put it-why should not farmers pursue the same method when they found they were overstocked with wheat or any commodity: reduce inventories and all will be well. I hope the Prime Minister will correct me if I am exaggerating in any way. To superficial hearers it seemed reasonable, but unfortunately it is not a parallel case at all. Business men can do that, even though it embarrasses the manufacturer, but when a farmer is invited to reduce his production of wheat there is a further question: what is he to do with his acreage? Either the Prime Minister did not think that a matter of concern or he overlooked it; at all events he did not enlighten the country or the farmers about it. That was an awful anti-climax to my right hon. friend's earlier dictum, when he said he was going to blast his way into the markets of the world. One could imagine all things that stood in the Prime Minister's way blowing up sky high. But now he says in effect: This blasting process has not worked out; the only way to meet the situation is not to
4592	COMMONS
Supply-International Wheat Agreement
have so much wheat to sell, and then I shall hot have to use so much powder in blasting. He said further: Would it not be better to sell one bushel of wheat at one dollar per bushel than two bushels at fifty cents each? That was intended to be a clincher. I was up in Mackenzie riding at the time-you heard about the Mackenzie by-election last fall no doubt, Mr. Speaker. When we arrived there it was terribly wet; all meetings were cancelled because of the condition of the roads. In Wadena we assembled in a room in the hotel where there was a radio and were entertained hearing this or another speech from Winnipeg by the Prime Minister. It was not a question whether he was reported properly or not; we were delighted to hear him, and we were almost convince! against our judgment that the Prime Minister had the remedy,-selling one bushel at one dollar instead of two at fifty cents each. If it were only as simple as that, wouldn't it be glorious? But there were one or two difficulties. To begin with, who was to give us the one dollar? And the statement was chock full of other economic blunders and fallacies, in addition to that vital defect. Mr. McFarland has never been able to dispose of his wheat at one dollar since then nor any one else in Canada that we have heard of. So the whole idea was just a dream and a mighty bad dream. Now what is the next move-the next part in the play? I have always believed that the Prime Minister himself never thought much of that wheat agreement. He has too good a business head to think that you can get prosperous by artificially reducing the world's production by practically endeavouring to shorten the arm of the Lord and reduce the abundance with which He has blessed this world. I could not imagine a man of parts like the Prime Minister preaching such a horrible, heathenish fallacy.
But, when we come to see who were his advisers on that occasion, then I am not so surprised at his blunder. Who were the Prime Minister's advisers at this international wheat conference and before? The three prairie premiers, Mr. Bracken on the east, Mr. Anderson in the centre and Mr. Brownlee on the western front. In addition he had Hon. Mr. MacPherson, a very fine and capable attorney general for Saskatchewan, who I remember went overseas with the Prime Minister. Then there was a gentleman familiarly known as Andy Cairns. He was there as a statistician. Those were the Prime Minister's advisers on this problem of an agreement to control the international marketing of wheat, restricting it to what were thought to be the consumpfMr. Motherwell.]
tive requirements of the world. Mr. Bracken made as good a case as could be made for an international agreement. He is the only farmer premier I know of in Canada,-I have not even that before me, because I did not know I would be speaking now. I followed him with a great deal of interest, particularly as Mr. Bracken was at one time a member of my own staff in Regina when I was a minister there. I knew him well; knew he was well informed, and his attitude had quite an effect upon me. I dug into the question further and further to see where he was wrong, if be were wrong, or if he were right wasn't it time I should get right and try to get behind this new theory of restricting our abundance in order that we might become wealthy. Might I point out incidentally that a while ago someone said that the man who could make two blades of grass grow where formerly there was one, such a one was the man of the hour, but now it seems that the man who would and could make one blade grow where formerly two grew is the boy from Galway. The latter was the Prime Minister's position. Well, I do not think much of that attitude. It is a new doctrine to me and I cannot get reconciled to it. Anyhow Mr. Bracken was behind it, Mr. Cairns was behind it; I understand it was he who gave Mr. Bracken the wrong slant. Mr. Cairns is a wizard with figures; he was adviser to the pool in the fall of 1929 as a statistician, but he is not an agricultural economist; that is something Mr. Cairns knew nothing about. But he can handle figures in a marvellous way; he seems to be able to mesmerize even those who should know better and convince them that he is also an authority on agricultural economics, which he is not. Consequently that adviser was never able to put my right hon. friend aright in the matter of what might come out of a world wheat agreement.
Then there was Mr. MacPherson, who went over with the Prime Minister. I know him very well; he was my opponent in the federal contest of 1921, when I got to know him very well and very favourably. But bless your heart, Mr. Speaker, what he did not know about wheat would fill a whole book and more. How could he possibly know anything about wheat? How could you expect to take a professional man, I don't care how high he is in his profession, and trot him off to a world conference expecting him to work out one of the biggest problems that was ever attempted to be worked out in connection with any farm commodity? Bread is spoken of as the staff of life, and here this uninitiated lawyer attempted to work out this great

Supply-International Wheat Agreement
problem. I am not saying anything disrespectfully of lawyers; I would say the same thing of myself if I were put into some job I knew nothing about and expected to make a good job of it. I did not expect him to be of much use to the Prime Minister, and he was not; it was a case of the blind leading the blind, because on that wheat question they were both as blind as bats.
Now we come to Doctor Anderson, also a man of parts. I suppose he had more of a cosmopolitan education than Mr. MacPherson had; he was also a lawyer and he held an honorary doctor's degree. He was some man, but he did not know very much about wheat either. It would be difficult for anyone to live in the west without knowing a field of wheat when it was growing, but I have seen men come from eastern Canada who did not know a field of wheat when it was growing. Certainly Doctor Anderson was not qualified to give much good advice to the Prime Minister. Then there was the third prairie premier, Hon. Mr. Brownlee, another gentleman of parts, another lawyer, head of the farmer's government out there for a long time. He was very acceptable in that capacity but, notwithstanding his many qualifications, no one ever dreamed that he knew much about an international wheat agreement. I realize that he has been mentioned in connection with many appointments, but he lacked the one thing that was necessary in an effective adviser to the Prime Minister of Canada on such an important errand.
With all those advisers, or misadvisers, is it any wonder that the thing did not go? It did go in a sense; it went from bad to worse, and now it is about on the scrap heap. A wheat agreement including certain quotas that did not include Russia was a very defective agreement. No matter how she talked how could you expect a great, proud nation like Russia to agree to any such thing? She was coming along with a constitution and form of government that many of us did not like, but it was her prerogative to have any kind of government she preferred so long as it did not interfere with other countries. They were building up their country and we slapped them bang in the face with these embargoes. Then we expected the representatives of that great country to play Canada's game in connection with an agreement concerning wheat, with Russia on the up grade, developing her wheat in order to feed her own people, who were increasing in number very rapidly due to the natural increase. It was an act of childish folly for anyone to expect Russia to sign that quota agreement; it was contrary
to the very nature of things. She was going onward and upward in wheat production and Canada was the last country that had any right to expect her to come down off her pedestal and adapt herself to our requirements with respect to wheat production.
That was the beginning of the let-down. It was true that the Danubian countries signed the quota agreement; Argentine signed, and Canada and the United States signed. Practically all the important countries signed with the exception of Russia, but it was not long before the Argentine showed signs of wanting to get out of it. Their crop was larger than they had expected; their quota was only something like 110,000,000 bushels, and it became rumoured that the Argentine had changed her mind, which might be expected in any democratic country. Sometimes governments are compelled to change their attitude. I am not criticising the Argentine; I have no doubt she changed her mind because her people changed their minds, but the result is that she is sailing ahead above her quota without regard to the wheat agreement at all. Sihe has exceeded her quota now by some six or seven million bushels, and by the end of the present grain year she is expected to be something like forty million bushels ahead of her quota. I understand that she entered into some negotiations with the continuing committee in London, but that she did not say one thing or the other; she just went on sawing wood, or in other words exporting wheat, and she is not under the agreement now either technically or otherwise.
May I ask who was the first defaulter? Did not Canada default the moment she neglected to have this parliament concur in that agreement? I am not an international diplomat or authority, but I have been in politics for some time, and I have never seen an agreement come back either to a legislature or to this parliament which was not presented for concurrence or disapproval, as might be thought best. Invariably it was the government of the day that negotiated the agreement; invariably the government of the day was supported, but this agreement has not been supported or concurred in nor has this house been asked to do so. We were asked to concur in the silver agreement arrived at during the course of the same conference; so that a less important agreement was concurred in by this parliament, yet until to-day we have not been given an opportunity of discussing the more important agreement, so far as I know. We set a day apart to discuss sweepstakes, which surely are not of as much importance as an international

Supply-International Wheat Agreement
wheat agreement. We discussed that subject for a whole day, and I think to advantage, but we were not given a day to discuss this agreement. It is up to the right hon. Prime Minister to explain these things. It is just possible that there may be an alibi, and if there is I think it is the duty of the Prime Minister to seek an opportunity to explain that alibi instead of waiting for me to bring up and press the matter.
I want to be able to go home and either say that the wheat agreement was concurred in by the parliament of Canada or that there was some sound reason for not asking concurrence. I think I know the reason. It began to dawn upon the right hon. Prime Minister, as it has been dawning upon the rest of us, that he was wrongly advised, so what did he do? He said in effect to the prairie premiers. "You have shoved me into this thing; now I am just going to pass the buck back to you and 'let George do it.' " The three Georges have been trying to do it ever since; they passed an act in each province allocating this 200,000,000 bushel quota of ours. Well, we are away below even the quota now and the grasshoppers are making it appear that we will hardly require a quota this year or next. The only excuse the Argentine gives for default, so far as I have seen, is that Canada did not live up to her agreement to reduce acreage. I do not know that Canada ever agreed actually to reduce the acreage; I do not know. That has been said, and that inference has been drawn. When you , reduce exports however-and we have agreed to reduce exports-you must admit that inferentially it means a reduction of acreage. Otherwise you will have the excess production backed up on the hands of the farmers. Can the farmer pay his bills by looking at his wheat in rickety old granaries not fit to take care of it in the summer time, granaries in many instances with rats in the bottom and cracks in the sides?
That is the wonderful policy which the right hon. gentleman opposite evolved. I am looking forward to the Prime Minister telling me how he can justify not asking for concurrence, and still claiming that he played the game. As I see it, he was the first to default, on behalf of Canada-not counting Kussia. She did not default, because she never agreed to her quota. If the Prime Minister will show substantial reasons why he did not ask concurrence I shall remove that harsh word. If you like, I shall remove it now. Probably I should wait until he makes his presentation of the case, and probably I should not be so harsh as even to suggest that Canada defaulted in her interna-

tional obligations. But how can I get away from it? That is the excuse the Argentine gave; they said that Canada did not come to the scratch, and therefore they wanted to know why they should be expected to toe the mark. That is the way the matter stands. We will soon be out of the present crop year. The stabilization authority in Winnipeg has been very desirous of holding up the price, and for that attitude I must give him credit. I have pointed out on three or four occasions however that the moment you hold the price of a commodity out of line with those of your competitor, then your export sales weaken and dribble off. That is what happens and has happened in Canada. Apparently we are not going to get our quota of 200,000,000 bushels filled during the present year and with an estimated 160 millions or more of a carry-over on August next. It is a very laudable effort on the part of Mr. McFarland; He wants to get a price for the farmer, and I commend that attitude. We would certainly be glad to get a better price, but we would be gladder still to get more sales also. Are we going to be hamstrung like this in an agreement on which everybody else defaults even if I admit we may not have defaulted? As soon as it becomes embarrassing they say in effect, "Well, good-bye Mary Jane; I am off this quota business; anybody who likes can stay on." It is time we had a statement from the Prime Minister about this matter, and he should not have waited until the end of the session to make it. He looked as mad as a hatter or a March hare on Saturday night because some of us wanted to know a few things which we would not have known if prorogation had taken place then.
There is another phase of the matter about which I should like to make only a few observations. Who will say that even if we could have a practical international reduction wheat agreement, that is the right policy for us to persue. I put a resolution on the order paper a year ago last February asking this government to institute an inquiry into the possibility of selling more wheat and wheat flour in China. We were evidently being crowded out of Europe. The government were going to shut, indeed were shutting, their eyes to the possibilities of other markets. We could have looked for a market in China, and it was wrong, absolutely wrong before man and God, to try to reduce production when there were millions, tens of millions, hundreds of millions of people throughout the world going to bed hungry. Yet we did not even make an attempt to barter wheat with

Supply-International Wheat Agreement
thena for their goods. We did not send a commission, a committee or even a single minister to the orient to see what was going on, and to learn if something could not be done to sell our wheat. I would not be surprised if a famine visited this old world; it almost looks that way even now. If man is not ingenious enough, after the showers of food blessings which have been bestowed upon him, to make a better job of distributing than he is doing now, it will be like when the manna fell from heaven and a lot of those lazy old. Jews would, not even gather up enough on Saturday night to do them over Sunday. Do you think they deserved to have more manna, under the circumstances? No, let them starve someone avers; that would have been more like justice. If we always had full justice meted out to us I do not know whether we would even be here or not. We hope the justice will not be meted out to us that we sometimes bring down upon ourselves. But this government uses all the ingenuity at its command to lessen the abundance, to create artificially higher prices so that those who had abundance would get more therefor, and so that those who had little or nothing would not be able to buy that which was offering at even the low prices hitherto prevailing. What a great policy in a Christian country! Apparently there is no recognition of the fact that there is a Great Architect or Wheels* man at the helm of it all, but they-the twenty-one countries so engaged-just go along and say, "I will fix that up; I will artificially reduce the arm of the Lord in the matter of abundance." I can tell you it is being reduced all right, both in Europe and on this continent. But practically none of it is now going to China, as a result of the policies of my right hon. friend opposite.
I have been trying to learn what was done in the matter of wheat sales to China. For nearly five months I have been making constant inquiries. The government of my right hon. leader did not send the Hon. Mr. Marler to Tokyo as an ornament. He has been making reports, some of which I have seen. Of course I have not seen the inside of them. When officials representing the Hon. Mr. Stevens came to see me, to ascertain what would fill my order for a return, they showed me a number of documents, a whole lot of them, and they told me that two reports on wheat had been made by the Hon. Mr. Marler, respecting the possibilities of selling more wheat flour and wheat in China. I said that was all I wanted, and told them not to ask me to read the rest in order to get at those two. They went away quite happy.
I know those reports are in existence, and the Prime Minister has indicated that they are private. He did not say whether or not they were marked "private" by the Hon. Mr. Marler; I venture to say that they were not marked private, at all by him. No doubt those documents refer to one of the subjects uppermost in Mr. Marler's mind when he went to China. I happened to be in Vancouver immediately before he sailed, and having held conversation with him I know what was uppermost in his mind. He went to be a real emissary to get contacts with the eastern world whereby Canada would be able to sell more of her wheat, and other commodities. The Prime Minister-and I suppose he has a right to do so-has said that those reports cannot be tabled. I will go farther, and recognize his right to take that action, despite the fact that they may not have been sent as private and confidential; or that they may not have been marked "private." I recognize his right to make them private, and so to mark them. They could be considered private from his standpoint, and I am not finding any fault with him in that respect. He could mark them as being private information and then pass them on to the department interested, namely the Department of Trade and Commerce. Under instructions from his leader the Minister of Trade and Commerce could not, under the circumstances, table the reports, and that is the reason I have not been demanding them recently.
We have been kept in the dark long enough, and that is why I am availing myself of this opportunity of bringing the matter to the attention of the house and the country generally. I think it would have been better for the Prime Minister if he had brought down the return I asked for on February 9 last, and given the people an opportunity to see whether or not Mr. Marler was performing his duty, or whether the government had failed to carry out its duties. Then we want to know which should be dismissed, and if either had been negligent. That is all we want to know. We have not been given that opportunity. I have nothing more to say at this time, except to express the hope that this appeal, which I expect will be the last one this session, may be answered. I hope that even yet the Prime Minister will clear the skirts of Canada by taking the responsibility of either asking this house to concur in this quota agreement or at least showing mighty good cause why it should not be concurred in if it is to remain in effect.

Mr. Speaker, when a week ago

I asked this house whether or not it was thought to be desirable that we should have three sittings a day and close the business by sitting on Saturday, the house unanimously expressed the view that I should take the action which I subsequently did by preparing the motion which was submitted to this chamber and unanimously adopted. The further question that has been raised as to the wisdom or unwisdom of there being a lessening in production is a matter that can always be discussed. It is a debatable question, and I am not going to say again what has been said so frequently, and what I did say in Winnipeg, that when a man finds himself producing in larger quantities than he is able to sell, and which he knows he cannot sell because the people who used to buy from him are supplying themselves, when fifty million acres that used to be sown to cereals were put out of production during the great war, and forty millions were added to production in the United States and ten millions in this country, it follows that as soon as the country that was out of production went back into production

there would be a corresponding loss of opportunity on the part of the United States and of Canada to sell their cereals where they had sold them during the war and immediately thereafter.
Just as soon as the devastation caused by the war was overcome and the communities . in question were able to sow and reap a harvest, just so soon was that market which Canada and the United States had theretofore enjoyed, limited to that extent.
So far as China is concerned we did have negotiations and we were offered, as I told this house many months ago, an opportunity to sell wheat to China on three-year terms,
I think it was; -but the conditions of government in China were such that we did not on that ground think it was desirable. But there was something more. They only desired to pay for the wheat a price equal to what our lowest grade of wheat would sell at, and we could not reduce the price of wheat in this country to less than forty cents a bushel in order to accept the Chinese offer, and we did not do so. The soft wheat of other countries found a more ready market than we were able to compete with. The price of wheat on the world market by reason of conditions that have been brought about partly by the agreement, partly by climatic conditions, partly by the acts of nature, and partly by grasshoppers, has been enhanced by these conditions, and I can only say to the hon. gentleman that it does appear to me to be-well, I shall not use the word I was going to use on this my birthday; I will only say that it does seem incredible that with knowledge of conditions as to the area that was put out of wheat raising and the increased areas that were put into wheat on the North American continent and in other parts of the world as well, when those countries went back to producing wheat to expect that we could sell them the wheat that we had been selling them while they were devastated.
In China the conditions of government are such that whether it is the government of Nanking or some other government that you are going to deal with you do not know what the conditions will be. Private purchasers have acquired wheat from Canada but the only offer which China made to this country in consequence of negotiations and inquiries and investigations was an offer to buy wheat at a price that we would not accept if we had the wheat to sell and at a price that we would not ask those who owned it to accept, and in addition they contemplated payment over a long term of years, necessitating that the dominion government finance the transaction in the meantime to provide the purchase price to those who sold. I am not unmindful that when the hon. gentleman first discussed a wheat conference at Regina he said, and the first literature that was prepared indicated, that all Canada had now to do was to produce, produce, produce, and many accepted his statement-

That was a very reasonable mistake to make, I suppose, but it was made. So far as we are concerned we have endeavoured by every means within our power to bring home to the Canadian people the fact that in the countries in which formerly they sold their product they can no longer sell it for the simple and obvious reason that those countries all over Europe-down the Danubian basin, in Hungary, France and elsewhere, and in the Czechoslovakian countries, in all that territory where grain was produced in such abundance before the war, and which with the war was devastated- once more began to produce: the hardy peasants, finding how few of them relatively were left, as compared with their numbers before the war, prepared the soil for wheat, with renewed energy, and reaped an abundant harvest by their labour. arise from the fact that Europe is now in production to a larger extent than before, or at least since the days of the great war. The amazing thing to me is that climatic conditions have played an important part in reduction in Canada and helped the situation tremendously. I wonder what would have happened to the Canadian farmer if we had produced at the same rate as we did in 1926, 1927 and 1928. Yet the right hon. gentleman seems to forget that the one country upon whom we could depend, or rather group of countries, Great Britain and the empire, for the absorption of our surplus wheat production, we have taken action against by way of tariffs, imposed in 1930 and 1931. The result is that to-day, even with depleted production, we are piling up surpluses every year. In view of the tariff increases against imports of British goods into Canada, can anyone blame Mr. Elliot and his propaganda for independence of any of the empire countries?" Not a particle, when the empire countries treat Great Britain in the manner this government has done. While we have no claim on European countries, any trading we have done with them has been largely due to the fact that they required our product; and when owing to climatic conditions, the very best quality of wheat produced in Canada has been almost nil during the past three years, this government finds itself in the unhappy position of having piled up a larger surplus than any other wheat exporting country in the world. Yet hon. gentlemen opposite will tell us and the electorate that there was nothing they could do. The thing is perfectly absurd. There is a great deal that this government could have done and has refused to do, and I want to make this statement now in the House of Commons because I am going to make it on a great many platforms in Canada; and I am serving notice on the government that it will be made in no uncertain terms. So far as the farmers of this country are concerned, apart from granting relief, which I admit the government has done in a generous way, my hon. friends have done nothing, which they can name, that has been of the slightest assistance in selling the export products of Canada.
Mr. THOMAS F. DONNELLY (Willow Bunch): Three things are disturbing the farmers of western Canada: first, our climatic conditions; secondly, a market for our products; and thirdly, debt adjustment. We believe that this government has done much to injure the market for our products. The one thing we have to sell chiefly in the markets of the world is our wheat. When the Liberal

government came in in 1921 we were shipping between 200 and 300 million bushels, and in 1929 we were shipping 407 million bushels. Since that time the market for our wheat has gradually dwindled until this year, with a quota of 200 million bushels, we shall not be able to fill our quota. Year by year the market for our wheat has grown smaller and smaller, and the explanation is to be found in the trade policies of this government. Not long ago there was a conference at Rome attended by all the exporting countries and by practically all the importing countries, and one importing country which in the past has used a great deal of Canadian wheat gave us the answer then. France said: "We are willing to take off the restrictions we have imposed on Canadian wheat; we would like to take the duty off your wheat and are willing to buy it from you, but what will you buy from us in exchange for it"? The hon. gentleman (Mr. Donnelly) has referred to France. I sat down on one occasion with twelve or fifteen gentlemen representing four or five departments of the government of France, to negotiate a treaty with that country. When it came to the discussion of wheat I was pressing for the admission on favourable terms of Canadian wheat into the French market and I was very insistent. One gentleman, I think it was the representative of the Department of Agriculture asked: "Mr. Cahan, do you know anything of French history?" I said that I knew something of French history as a schoolboy and as a student at college, and I knew something of her later history. "Well," he said, "if you have studied French history you will know that for four and a half centuries no man in France has reached the age of sixty years and certainly not sixty-five years who has not seen this country overrun with foreign troops." He said: "We no longer are able to maintain a fleet that will safeguard the carrying of wheat to France from Argentina, Australia and Canada in case of war. We have learned

by experience, and the policy of the French government and of all governments in France will be to produce sufficient wheat in France to maintain its population in case another crisis should arise in Europe." He said: "It is useless to present to us any arguments to the contrary." Then as I proceeded to urge that the use of strong or hard wheat was necessary in that country for mixing purposes, one of his assistants said: "But we are producing all the hard wheat that is necessary for French consumption." I asked: "Where?" He said, "For some years we have been importing from Saskatchewan hard wheat, sowing it in our North African provinces and producing there as good quality of hard wheat as you produce in Saskatchewan." He said: "We had available last year of hard wheat from the North African colonies 25,000,000 bushels for sale in France, and we must give prior advantage in our market to our Algerian colonies." One gentleman sitting beside him, a more elderly man-I remember his name but I shall not repeat it-said: "Perhaps you are misleading Mr. Cahan in this discussion, because although we imported hard wheat from Saskatchewan and sowed it, in the first year we produced equally good wheat as that of Saskatchewan, and from the seed of that crop there was equally good wheat the following year, yet in the third or fourth years the wheat tends to deteriorate and become soft, and we may have to import hard wheat from your country for our sowing every third or fourth year. But outside that you cannot hope for any large market for your wheat in France." Then, turning to the statistics, he showed me that for the previous year they had produced in France alone outside its colonies within sixty million bushels of the total product of Canada from sea to sea, and that for that year, according to the returns which were in then, they were producing more wheat in France alone than we had produced in the whole of Canada in the previous year. Under those circumstances it does not become a question of tariffs; it becomes, on the part of France, a grave question of national policy, based upon a clear determination on the part of successive governments and of all parties in France to raise in that country, at no matter what cost, sufficient wheat to feed their own people.
In Switzerland much the same situation exists. The Swiss regulations against the importing of foreign wheat have absolutely nothing to do with the tariff in Canada on Swiss products, but are due to the demand of the Swiss agriculturists that they shall be so protected and bonused as to enable them to supply from their own cultivated lands the
[Mr. Donnelly.j

There was undoubtedly on Saturday night some natural resentment in our not getting away, but it was perhaps hardly fair that the Minister of Justice should blame us for holding the house over. The fact is that we had a great deal of work to do. The Prime Minister had taken a chance on business being through by ten o'clock. The Liberals took their full share in discussing various items before we reached the estimates for penitentiaries. Under the circumstances it seemed to me that the only thing to do was to insist on securing fuller information from the minister than had yet been given to the house. I recognize clearly that the minister is not personally to blame for what we believe to be the bad conditions in Kingston penitentiary. However, under our procedure there seems to be no other way of getting at the facts than by insisting that the minister give us fuller explanation than the house or the country have yet received. I would point out that the prisoners are the most defenceless class in the community. They have been deprived of the ordinary rights of citizenship. They have no means of making their grievances known to this house. They have even been deprived of the rights of normal ordinary human beings.
They are not normal human beings.

That is true, but I say, being deprived of the rights of normal human beings it seems to me .that that is

Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries
all the more reason why we should see that no injustice is done to them. I think every one recognizes the difficulty of getting at the facts in a matter of this kind. On the one hand there is not the slightest doubt that we must discount the statements that come from ex-convicts; they are likely to be biased. But on the other hand I am coming to believe that we must discount to a considerable extent the official statements, the official denials, because it seems to have been the policy more or less to whitewash underofficials. I hope that is not true, but again and again we have had statements made that everything was going very well, only to learn a few weeks later that things were not satisfactory at all. We were told a few days ago that the resignation of Colonel Megloughlin was enforced because he had not been doing satisfactory work. It seems to me that that is hardly sufficient in view of the long history of trouble that there has been at that penitentiary. There are many who feel that in this case Colonel Megloughlin has been made the goat for inefficiency on the part of other officials, or perhaps for the lack of proper policy on the part of the department. It is for these reasons that we in this corner urge the appointment of a royal commission. We believe that this situation ought to be cleaned up. We believe that the public have the right to know the actual situation. It is difficult, as I have said, for the public to get accurate knowledge either from those who have been in the penitentiary or on the other hand from officials whose positions may be at stake. It is only by sending in absolutely impartial investigators that we shall get satisfactory results. Furthermore we urge that the time has come when there should be general consideration of the whole question of prison administration and the treatment of criminals. Other countries in the past have treated criminals more or less as we are doing to-day. Great Britain is an outstanding example of a country which at last realized that something was necessary. A royal commission was appointed, following which certain definite lines of reform were introduced; it is not necessary to go into that now. But if Great Britain found it necessary to make a thorough investigation and to reform the whole policy of dealing with prisoners, I think it is high time that we in Canada should follow suit.
I take it that in a general way crime is the result either of heredity or of bad environment. If it is a result of heredity perhaps the time has come that we must consider whether we should go on producing criminals, whether there should not be some
effort made in the case of bad strains either to segregate or to sterilize those who may produce criminals-
To apply quotas.

No. My hon. friend behind me is making light of the question. I say that anyone who has made any study of heredity knows that there are people who are subnormal and some proportion of whose descendants will be subnormal. In that case it seems to me a crime that we should permit those people to propagate. Either they should be sterilized or segregated so that they could not produce children. I am not discussing to-day which course should be taken. But we have in our prisons large numbers of people who, if I may use the phrase, are bom criminals. It is high time to remedy that situation. When men are known to be criminal, incorrigible as the minister points out, it seems to me that these men ought not to be turned loose again in the community after a few years' sentence. It is not that I would make the punishment more severe, but I would provide more effectively for the protection of society. If they are really incorrigible they ought never to be released. They may be treated with kindness and fairness, but they should be kept always apart from other members of society and not allowed either to injure society or to reproduce their kind.
But I take it that the great majority of prisoners are criminals not because of bad heredity but because of certain bad influences and surroundings. There is no doubt that when we have a large volume of unemployment the curve of crime goes up. That indicates a close connection between unemployment and crime. It would seem to me that the thing for us to do is not to build bigger and better prisons but rather to study closely the conditions that produce crime. Then coming to the individual, I do not think the treatment for criminals should be the same in every case. I know of boys being sent to reformatories, without the superintendent in charge being given any indication at all by the judge as to the boy's background, but only the statement of the crime committed. In the case of one boy it might be a first offence, with another it might be the result of very bad environment, and with another almost a chance occurrence. The treatment should vary accordingly.
So I urge that we have a royal commission to study not merely the actual situation in Kingston penitentiary but also to put us in

Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries
the way of adopting more modern and humane and intelligent methods of dealing with criminals.
The minister the other day very definitely accepted responsibility for the recent punishment of a number of convicts. It seems that on the occasion of the visit of the Governor General to Kingston there was what the minister characterized as a noisy outbreak. As a result twenty-two men were awarded corporal punishment. Two of them, I think the minister said, were found to be medically unfit to sustain this punishment; the others got what is known as the paddle. I would submit that such severe punishment, if it is ever necessary, should be reserved for very serious crimes, and not be inflicted merely for breaches of prison discipline. I think if any of us were imprisoned and thus deprived of our liberty, and felt that there was a grievance-as these men felt there was a great grievance, and as it has been since acknowledged that there was a grievance,-we would take whatever means we had at our disposal to bring that grievance to the notice of the public. The fact that they beat some tin pans or did something of the sort when the Governor General was in Kingston was no very serious crime; it was merely a natural way of calling their grievances to the attention of the public, and I do submit that the very severe form of punishment known as paddling was altogether too drastic for such infringement of the prison regulations.
The minister told us that recently attempts were made to give the prisoners outdoor exercise. which developed into Sunday games to which the church goers took objection; they did not want to hear this noise on the Lord's day. It does occur to me, Mr. Chairman, that if people in the vicinity objected to the noise on the Lord's day the officers in charge very easily might have altered the time for these outdoor exercises or this recreation to some other day than Sunday. Most of the men are not. working steadily; it is merely a matter of adjustment of the ordinary routine of prison life, and to one on the outside it would seem that it might be possible to give reasonable outdoor exercise on some other day than Sunday. To me that little incident seems typical of the regimentation we have there, the inelasticity of the discipline, and the unnecessary harshness of prison routine.
Now I come to the charges made by Major Niclde which, since I read his letter the other day, he has said that he is quite ready to substantiate. The other day I suggested to the minister that these were so serious in their character that it seemed to me that if

any of them were untrue he ought to make a definite, categorical denial. Major Nickle says there is a form of punishment under which men have their hands raised about their heads; they are shackled to the bars, confined for seven or fourteen days and fed on bread and water.
That has been abolished.

I should like to
know if that punishment has been abolished, as my hon. friend from Southeast Grey suggests; if it has been abolished, I should like to know when that was done. Was it abolished because of the protests of the prisoners? If it was considered right to abolish this form of punishment had not the protests of the prisoners real, substantial grounds, and why should we inflict upon them such severe punishment for protesting against what is now considered to be an altogether unjustifiable form of punishment?
I have already referred to paddling, and the minister has said that paddling is not administered now except by order of the department. I should like to ask him whether there are very definite criteria by which he judges whether or not this punishment should be inflicted, or whether the appeal to Ottawa is a perfunctory matter, as is so often the case in such affairs.
Further with regard to sanitary matters there is a very serious charge that people who have active syphilis bathe in the same tubs as other prisoners. I should like to ask definitely whether this situation has been altered and, if so, when. I cannot see that there ever could have been any reason for allowing a practice of this kind.
Further than that, have any real attempts been made at segregating youthful offenders? Some years ago some of us understood, when Collins Bay was being established, that it was for youthful offenders. Later I believe the minister denied that this was really the purpose, and stated that it was for certain preferred classes. The house will recall that a year or two ago attention had to be directed to the fact that apparently brokers were among the preferred classes, since they were placed at Collins Bay. I want to know whether, after all these years, during which royal commissions from time to time have made their reports and there have been protests in this house, there is any definite program before the minister with regard to segregating youthful offenders. Again Major Nickle says that of the total number of prisoners only some 125 are given a chance to learn a trade. Again

Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries
and again it has been stated that at least one of the purposes of the penitentiary was to enable the criminal to become a respectable citizen once more. I wonder whether it is possible for men who are confined for several years, some of them for a greater number of years, to become respectable citizens and hope to again enter the normal life of the country if they are given no chance whatever to learn a trade while in the penitentiary. I know perfectly well that there are some difficulties in the way. A few years ago some of us were waited upon by some of the penitentiary officials asking that something should be done through which greater facilities for work might be afforded. I know there are certain difficulties in the way, but I do not think they are insuperable. With all the work that might be done in this country it seems to me some arrangement might be made under which the majority of the prisoners could learn trades or engage in suitable work. It may be that nothing could be done with the hundred in-corrigibles to whom the minister referred, but what about the other six or seven hundred prisoners, many of whom are young people, who to-day have no opportunity of fitting themselves for their future life outside the penitentiary walls?
And that is just one penitentiary.

Yes; I am glad that my hon. friend reminds me that I am speaking of only one penitentiary. There are somewhat similar conditions existing in other penitentiaries, though I think in some of the others more has been done in the way of providing outdoor work.
Then there is another specific charge with regard to one John O'Brien. It was stated that he had been in solitary confinement since 1931. I think the house is entitled to know whether he is still in solitary confinement and, if not, when he was released, and in any case why he was kept there during those years. It is a very serious matter especially, as I say, for men who have no means of getting their grievances before the general public.
Then we come to another question, that of (political prisoners. The minister may say that we have no political prisoners in Canada, but I think that is a statement that can hardly be made good, because the seven communists who are in Kingston to-day, of whom I think two have been released recently because of poor health-
Mr. GUTHRIE; No, that is not so.
I will leave the minister to explain the reason; I was giving him credit for kindheartedness.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Their health is good.

In any case these communists are there because of their political beliefs. I am not going to deal with that clause of the criminal code under which they were arrested, except to say that under that clause a man need not be guilty of committing any overt crime. He need only belong to a party which advocates the use of force to bring about political change. These men were not convicted of any overt crime. They were not charged with an overt crime, but were charged simply with belonging to an association which in turn was affiliated with another association which believed in force as a means of bringing about political change. I quite recognize that in mentioning the communists I immediately lay myself open to the criticism of being in sympathy with them. I have stated again and again in this House of Commons, and I wish to state once more that I have no connection whatever with the communist party and no sympathy with the tactics they pursue. Further, let me point out that according to a report in the Toronto Daily Star of Monday, February 19, Mr. A. E. Smith stated at Massey Hall that representatives of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in the House of Commons were responsible for the charges of sedition against him, as they suggested to the Bennett government that by means of a charge of this nature they could dispose of their political enemies and not have to resort to section 98 of the criminal code. Needless to say, members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in this house never gave any such advice to the Minister of Justice, nor have I ever held that in any sense of the word the Minister of Justice was responsible for the shooting at the cell of Tim Buck. I read the statement from the Toronto Daily Star simply to point out that hon. members in this comer of the house have been charged by the communists with bringing about the shooting. In this connection perhaps I should say Mr. Smith has stated he did not put it just that way. Very well; the fact is he never repudiated it. But whatever Mr. Smith actually did say, the communists have denounced us most bitterly. Notwithstanding that bitter denunciation I urge that prisoners should not be treated as apparently the communists in Kingston have been treated. Unless we agree with the kind of thing Hitler has been doing in Germany within the last few days, I would say that political prisoners have a right to
Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries

be protected, and that all people in Canada- Conservatives, Liberals and members in this comer-should try to retain the institutions of democracy and to resist the inroads of anything like a dictatorship. If we are convinced that we must pursue democratic principles I think we must ask for the protection of political prisoners. Further than that we may very well consider whether or not it is wise to continue to have on our statute books laws under which men may be convicted merely for holding certain political opinions which are not generally accepted.
One of these communists, namely Tim Buck, had shots fired into his cell. There are nearly nine hundred prisoners in the penitentiary. How is it that the cell selected for the shooting was one in which there was a communist? That does look as if they have been singled out for this peculiar kind of treatment. The other day the minister admitted that eleven shots were fired into Buck's cell. I submit that that incident has a very ugly look. I believe our papers right across the country have expressed themselves as being definitely opposed to that kind of treatment, and they have urged that the situation be cleaned up.
The other day the minister gave us the impression-certainly he gave me the impression-that the shooting took place at the time of the riot on October 17. I understand-and I should like the minister to correct me if I am wrong-that the shots were not fired until October 20. There is a discrepancy which ought to be cleared up. If the big riot took place on October 17, it is very strange that a man should be shot at by the guards three days later.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There was a much bigger riot on October 20.
I shall be glad to hear about that. I thought there was a riot on the 17th.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That was the start of it.

From what place
were the shots fired? I am informed they were not fired from inside the penitentiary, but that they were fired from outside.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is correct.

I hope the minister will clear up that matter. If there is a range of cells three stories high and there is one particular cell in which a prisoner is being confined, and if somebody outside marks that cell, and it is shot at, then I say that is a pretty deliberate act. It is a deliberate act, and requires some explanation. What was the

reason? The minister says the reason was to intimidate Tim Buck, and he states further that Tim Buck was exhorting the other prisoners to riot. I confess I am absolutely mystified by the contrast between the statement of the minister and the report of Judge Deroche, from which the hon. member for Southeast Grey read. In his judgment Judge Deroche said:
The men (meaning the inmates) had for months and possibly years been asking for the removal of certain grievances which were in their minds, with little or no response.
Then he goes on to say:
They now decided that on October 17, at three o'clock p.m. they would walk out of the shops and make a peaceful demonstration to impress the warden and through him Ottawa.
Then at page 7 he states:
Then to go back to the cause of the riot. This peaceful demonstration which developed into a riot, was for the purpose of emphasizing the demands of the men for redress of certain grievances which had been long and repeatedly denied them. Many of the grievances for which this demonstration was staged have already been granted to the men, proving conclusively to my mind that those demands must have been reasonable.
We have now from the Minister of Justice an entirely different view being conveyed to the house. At page 7 of the judgment Judge Deroche, with regard to Tim Buck, states as follows:
Buck told them-
That is the prisoners.

that the soldiers would not hurt them if they did no violence to person or injury to property.
Then again:
When it was announced that the soldiers were coming, one of the men, Tim Buck, advised the men that the soldiers could not or would not hurt them so long as they did no damage to property or violence to anyone, and instructed the men to gather pails of water and barricade the door, expecting to stand siege.
It is a very curious thing if, as is stated by the judge, Tim Buck took that stand and made those statements, that his cell should be selected three days later as the one into which were to be poured eleven shots. I remember in our childhood days we used to read the tales of Fenimore Cooper, and we learned it was the practice of the Indians in the olden days to tie a captured enemy to a tree and to fire arrows at him, seeing who could come nearest his head [DOT] without hitting him. It looks to me as if this practice has been translated into the more modern method of putting a man into a cell, caging him up and then firing at him. Surely human beings

Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries
are not animals. I do not think there is a single sportsman in this house who would undertake to shoot an animal by caging it up in a cell and then firing at it. There is something that needs explanation and I would ask the minister when he speaks to say very definitely who gave the order to fire. I do not think the minister himself did, but he is the responsible official, the head of the department, and it is possible for him to ascertain who gave the order. I think it is right that he should tell this house who gave the order to fire. If no such order was given I would ask, have the guards who fired those eleven shots been arrested and disciplined? Take the minister's own statement when he said that Tim Buck had been fired at. He said:
Buck was one of those who were encouraging the disorder. At the door of his cell he was making speeches and encouraging the rioters, and for the purpose of frightening him, I suppose, or cowing him, certain guards fired into the ceiling of his cell.
I suppose that somebody knowing he was at the door of his cell must have given the order to fire, and they chased away around outside the walls and then from outside the walls they fired up at him. I do not know very much about criminal trials but that does not seem to me a very natural sort of procedure. I could understand a guard in desperation perhaps firing into a crowd, but why some of the guards should go away around outside the walls and fire eleven shots into a prisoner's cell is an absolute mystery to me. The minister said:
At the door of his cell he was making speeches and encouraging the rioters, and for the purpose of frightening him, I suppose, or cowing him, certain guards fired into the ceiling of his cell. There can be no doubt that if any man had wanted to shoot Tim Buck he could have done so. The very fact that ten or eleven shots were fired and there was no harm to Tim Buck shows that they were not trying to hit him. He was there for anybody to shoot.
That is an astonishing statement for the minister to make, that a convict was in his cell for anybody to shoot.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If there had been any intention of doing so, and there was not.

Well, I hope there was not, but the question still remains, who gave the order to fire? If the firing was done by the guards without orders, then I ask have those guards been disciplined? It would seem to me that when guards are sometimes dismissed for minor offences, or without reason given, it would surely be a reason for dismissal if guards in a responsible position should on 74728-291
their own responsibility fire into a cell. But if the orders to fire were given, I should like to know what official gave those orders and when it became the practice in our prisons to adopt this form of intimidation. It is bad enough to flog a man, but surely it is not, even in European prisons, a customary means of punishment that guards can go outside the prison walls and take pot shots at a cell in which a political prisoner is confined. The whole matter has a very ugly look, and I hope for the sake of his own department as well as for the credit of the institution and the man at the head of it, that the minister make a statement that will clear up this matter.
Before I sit down I once more want to appeal to the minister, and I wish the Prime Minister were in his seat so I might appeal to him, that on the grounds of humanity we should not longer delay having a very careful inquiry into the situation, and further than that, that the government appoint a board or commission of very able men, men of experience and humanitarian views, to inquire into the whole matter of prison reform.

Mr. Chairman, I want if
I may to say just a word on this matter. Having had some considerable experience in connection with matters of this kind as crown attorney and prosecuting attorney for the county in which I live, I know something of both sides of this very difficult question. On the one hand crime must be put down in this country, and the people are entitled to protection against it. It is a very difficult matter to know when prosecuting criminals and dealing with them just when you can apply mild methods and when you must resort to the most rigorous methods possible. I happen to come from a section of the country where unfortunately most of the men who are in the penitentiary cannot say they are there because I defended them. On the contrary, I contributed when I was doing that kind of work to a good number going to these institutions. I do not know the man in question in this particular case, but I do want to say to the minister that I know something of his difficulties, and yet there is throughout the section of the country in which I live a very strong feeling that perhaps the possibilities of saving some of those who are not past saving are not being utilized to the best advantage in Kingston at the present time.

How would you save
them?



Supply-Justice-Penitentiaries

I would say to my hon.
friend, because I know he is humane, that he is not anxious that the younger men particularly should lose all chance of again becoming good citizens. I am sure that no one in the house would regret that more than my hon. friend, and there are a good number of these young men who are sent to the penitentiary who I do not believe should be allowed to associate with the hardened criminals. I believe it is possible to reclaim them by giving them a chance again to become good citizens, and if we err I think we should err on that side. Just where to draw the line it is difficult to say. It is pretty hard to draw the line between being too lenient towards somebody who will afterwards turn out to be a murderer and those who will profit by the chance that is given them.
But I would say this to the minister in just the minute I intend to devote to the subject, that I do think that an investigation by a royal commission into this matter would do a great deal to clear the air and would be in the interests of everybody concerned, including the minister himself and those who are associated with him in the administration of that institution.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Before we resume the work of the committee, I think that in fairness to those who are responsible for the conduct of government I should ask the house whether or not they believe it is possible to prorogue this house this afternoon. On the strength of last Monday's proceedings, by which we undertook to prorogue on Saturday, His Excellency made certain plans. He has intimated that any plans he makes must of course be subordinated to his duty with respect to prorogation; but the uncertainty that has now characterized our deliberations for so long should in some sense, it seems to me, be disposed of. I should like to know therefore whether in the opinion of the house it is possible to prorogue this afternoon; otherwise we will sit to-night at eight o'clock and presumably conclude by eleven, although I understand that one hon. member has said we cannot prorogue to-day. If that is in the mind of hon. members I should like to indicate to His Excellency that such is the opinion of the house.

The Prime Minister has asked a word from those who are

responsible for the conduct of government; I rather hesitate to say anything in the circumstances. He is the one who has to do with that phase of affairs, but so far as we of the opposition are concerned I am not aware of any reason why the house should not prorogue this evening. I believe the ex-Minister of Agriculture wishes to speak when supply is taken up in connection with Trade and Commerce estimates, and I understand that there are two other hon. members to my right who have something in particular on which they wish to speak. Apart from that however I am not aware that it is the intention of any other hon. members to participate at any length in debate. There may be; I cannot say. I do think however that so far as we are concerned the purpose will be served by having the proceedings arranged for immediately after eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Could it not be done after six?
So far as we alone are concerned, I should hope it might be arranged for five.

Inasmuch as I had something to do with prolonging the business of the house I am glad to say now that I do not want more than ten or fifteen minutes, and if the statement made by the Minister of Justice is satisfactory from my point of view I shall not need that much time.

Since I have to share the responsibility for holding up the proceedings on Saturday night, I must say distinctly that we cannot at this stage give guarantees as to how long things will take. It is not that we want to prolong the business of the house unnecessarily. We were prevented for nearly an hour from going on this morning and I am not blaming anyone, but that is the way it turned out, and I think we should have a full statement from the minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member realizes that the penitentiary estimates were held up on four distinct occasions merely for the convenience of those opposite, and normally they would have been disposed of weeks ago. Not to meet my convenience.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
You were not here when we were going on.

It might have been brought on any time in the last two weeks but for some reason or other, in the judgment of the government, it was left until the last on Saturday night. A number of other contentious items were put before us and precluded the discussion of these estimates on that occasion, and I think we have a perfect right as members of the house, in view of the importance of the question, to ask that we be not limited as to the time which this discussion will take.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No one disputes that
right at all; it is merely a question of endeavouring to carry out what was a general understanding. If it cannot be done it cannot be done.

I was not anxious to stay here over Sunday nor am I anxious to stay a minute longer than necessary to complete what I conceive to be the business of the house from my point of view. I want to get home; I have not seen my home for nearly six months, and I have as much to go home to as the average person in the way of attachment to home. But take the question of the international wheat agreement that we discussed this morning. How could I go home without having discussed it? And take what I propose to discuss with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the lost Chinese market; I do not see how I can forego saying something in that regard. This is _ the occasion on which we ventilate the grievances of subjects whom we represent and serve; it is a privilege handed down to us by the mother of parliaments, and if we do not avail ourselves of it we neglect our duty. With these qualifications, I will expedite prorogation as far as I can; but if it has to go to six or seven or eight o'clock then it is not my fault. Prorogation does not come first; the business of the country does. The facilities for prorogation are ready for the purpose and it is when we want them as a parliament that they should be used.
